ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> This study analyzes data from PD and healthy control (HC) participants enrolled in PPMI [13], a large, multicenter observational study designed to identify biomarkers of PD progression.

> At study entry, PD participants had early-stage, idiopathic PD, enrolled within two years of diagnosis, were not on medication for treatment of PD, had a dopaminergic deficit confirmed by imaging, and did not exhibit atypical parkinsonian syndromes [13].

> HC participants were age-and sexmatched to the PD group, had no neurological disorders, and had no first-degree family members with PD [13].

> All PPMI participants provided written informed consent according to the study protocol and applicable ethical regulations [13].

> At baseline, 17% of PD participants were using medication for constipation, increasing to 34% by year five.

> Gastrointestinal Dysfunction: PD participants had higher reporting of GI complaints compared to HC and the odds of experiencing gastrointestinal dysfunction (subscore > 1) changed differently over time between PD and HC cohorts (p = 0.011).

> P values were calculated using Student's two-sample t test or Welch's two-sample t test for continuous measures other than disease duration, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for disease duration, and Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical measures, as appropriate.( 2) Autonomic symptom severity is defined by the number of affected autonomic domains a participant had: none (0), mild (1-2), severe (>2).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Autonomic symptoms are common in Parkinson's disease (PD) and impact quality of life, with unclear relationship to motor and cognitive progression.
Objective: Characterize five-year progression of autonomic symptoms in early PD and their association with motor and cognitive outcomes.
Methods: We analyzed data from 874 PD participants and 252 healthy controls (HC) enrolled in Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI).

Autonomic symptoms were assessed annually over five years using Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease-Autonomic dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT); affected autonomic domains were defined as domain subscore >1.
text.formatted: Autonomic symptoms were assessed annually over five years using Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease-Autonomic dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT); affected autonomic domains were defined as domain subscore >1.

text.text: Clinical measures included MDS-UPDRS and Montreal Cognitive Assessment.
Generalized estimating equations evaluated longitudinal changes, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and comorbidities.

Results: At baseline, 71% of PD participants reported >1 affected autonomic domain, increasing to 85% among 287 PD participants with 5-year follow-up; HCs reporting >1 affected autonomic domain increased from 40% of participants at baseline to 46% among 145 participants with 5-year follow-up.

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder classically defined by motor symptoms of bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability [1].

text.text: However, PD is increasingly recognized as a multisystem condition with diverse non-motor symptoms that profoundly impact quality of life [1].

text.text: Among these, autonomic dysfunction, affecting cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, urogenital, thermoregulatory, and pupillomotor functions, is particularly prevalent and debilitating [2].

text.text: Studies estimate that 70-80% of PD patients experience autonomic symptoms, which can emerge early in the disease course, even preceding motor manifestations, and may predict faster progression [1, 3].

text.text: Despite its clinical significance, autonomic dysfunction remains understudied, with gaps in longitudinal data on symptom progression, pathophysiological mechanisms, and its relationship to motor and cognitive decline [3].
text.formatted: Despite its clinical significance, autonomic dysfunction remains understudied, with gaps in longitudinal data on symptom progression, pathophysiological mechanisms, and its relationship to motor and cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The pathophysiology of autonomic symptoms in PD involves both central and peripheral nervous system degeneration.

Alpha-synuclein aggregates, a hallmark of PD pathology, are found in autonomic nuclei and peripheral nerves [4], suggesting that autonomic pathways may serve as conduits for the spread of pathology from the gut or other peripheral sites to the brain [5].

text.text: In PD, cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction is driven primarily by postganglionic sympathetic denervation, which impairs baroreflex function and reduces norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals, resulting in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and inadequate vasoconstriction on standing [6].

text.text: Similarly, gastrointestinal disturbances like constipation are linked to enteric nervous system involvement, while urinary symptoms like urinary incontinence, urinary retention, voiding dysfunction, urgency and frequency stem from degeneration of Onuf's nucleus in the spinal cord [5].

text.text: These disruptions not only impair daily functioning but also exacerbate other non-motor symptoms, such as sleep disturbances and depression, further diminishing quality of life [1].

text.text: Existing research highlights critical gaps.

First, while cross-sectional studies document autonomic symptom prevalence, longitudinal data are sparse, limiting insights into temporal progression and its interaction with disease milestones [3, [7] [8] [9] [10].

text.text: Second, the contribution of specific comorbidities, such as cardiovascular and metabolic disorders, to autonomic symptoms remains poorly quantified, potentially confounding observed associations [11].

text.text: This study addresses these gaps by analyzing longitudinal data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort to track autonomic symptom progression over 5 years and its relationship to motor and cognitive trajectories.

Using the Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease-Autonomic Dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT) [12], we evaluate rates of change across six autonomic domains while adjusting for comorbidities and medication effects, providing a nuanced understanding of autonomic dysfunction's natural history.

text.text: Additionally, by correlating autonomic severity with dopaminergic imaging markers (i.e., DaTscan uptake in the striatum), we explore potential biomarkers for disease progression.
We also incorporate orthostatic vital signs as an objective measure of autonomic function.
These findings aim to inform early intervention strategies and personalized management approaches that can ultimately improve quality of life for individuals living with PD.

To analyze the longitudinal progression of autonomic symptoms, generalized estimating equations (GEEs) with a logit link were applied to evaluate whether the cohorts differed in their longitudinal trajectories under the assumption that the log odds of the response changed linearly over time.

Models were also adjusted for medication use (yes/no) and comorbidities (yes/no).
For MDS-UPDRS III (ON), the model also adjusted for levodopa equivalent dose (LED).
In both sets of models, the auto regressive working correlation structure was employed.
Wald tests were used to assess if the interaction term between group (i.e., cohort or baseline symptom severity) and time was statistically significant.
Time effect p-values were reported for all models, and separate time effects with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) in each group were also provided when the interaction term was significant.

To account for multiple comparisons, a Bonferroni corrected p-value (0.05 divided by the total number of comparisons in each table) was used for each group of outcomes, i.e., 0.05/10 = 0.005 for presence of autonomic symptoms and 0.05/7 = 0.007 for severity of autonomic symptoms in PD.
Although the Bonferroni method is very conservative, it was selected for simplicity.

Since this analysis is purely observational, interpretation of significant p-values prior to the Bonferroni adjustments (i.e., using the 0.05 significance level) are provided and may provide some clinically meaningful insight.
Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess whether differential availability of follow-up autonomic data may have influenced the study findings.
Baseline characteristics were compared between participants with PD with and without observed Year 5 autonomic data.

In order to evaluate the potential impact of informative drop-out on the results of our longitudinal models, we incorporated inverse probability weighting (IPW) into the generalized estimating equation (GEE) models evaluating longitudinal changes in clinical outcomes by baseline autonomic symptom severity groups in the PD cohort.
IPWs were calculated as the inverse of the estimated cumulative probability of having observed autonomic data at each follow-up visit.

These probabilities were estimated using visit-specific logistic regression models of the probability of being observed at a given visit conditional on baseline characteristics (age, sex, disease duration, and lowest putamen ratio) and prior-visit The resulting visit-level IPWs were applied in longitudinal GEE models detailed above.

text.text: At baseline, 71% of PD participants reported experiencing more than one affected autonomic domain, compared with only 40% in HC participants.
Over the five-year follow-up, the proportion of PD participants with more than one affected autonomic domain increased to 85%, whereas the HC also increased, but remained lower compared to PD at 46%.

text.text: At baseline, 17% of PD participants were using medication for constipation, increasing to 34% by year five.
Similarly, the percentage of PD participants taking medication for urinary dysfunction rose from 12% to 19%.
The use of medications for sexual dysfunction remained relatively stable in both cohorts, while no HC participants reported taking medication for hypotension at any time point.
These trends suggest an increasing need for pharmacological management of autonomic dysfunction in PD over time.

text.text: Cardiovascular comorbidities were the most prevalent, affecting 38% of PD participants at baseline and increasing to 53% by year five.
In contrast, metabolic and urinary comorbidities showed smaller increases over time.
The HC group exhibited a similar pattern, but with urinary comorbidities at a consistently lower prevalence compared to PD.
These findings underscore the progressive nature and more extensive involvement of autonomic systems in PD.

Every year, the estimated odds of experiencing sexual dysfunction changed (p = 0.017) by a multiplicative factor of 1.088 (95% CI: 1.015, 1.166).

This difference in odds appears to be more elevated in men where the odds of experiencing sexual dysfunction increased every year (p = 0.004) by a multiplicative factor of 1.135 (95% CI: 1.042, 1.237), compared to women who did not significantly change (p = 0.879) over time.

There was no significant difference in the odds of experiencing orthostatic hypotension between PD and HC participants over time (p = 0.054), and every year, the estimated odds of experiencing orthostatic hypotension did not significantly change (p = 0.790).

text.text: This study, using data from a large cohort of early, de novo Parkinson's disease participants with positive CSF SAA (PPMI) [13], demonstrates that autonomic symptoms in PD progress steadily over a 60-month period.
text.formatted: This study, using data from a large cohort of early, de novo Parkinson's disease participants with positive CSF SAA (PPMI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, demonstrates that autonomic symptoms in PD progress steadily over a 60-month period.

text.text: Gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms were the most prominent and burdensome autonomic disturbances, with a notable increase in gastrointestinal dysfunction observed over time.
The reliance on medications, particularly those addressing constipation and urinary issues, increased as the disease advanced, reflecting the escalating severity of autonomic disturbances.
The presence of comorbidities-especially cardiovascular, metabolic, and urinary disorders-may further exacerbate autonomic symptoms and contribute to greater symptom severity.
Urinary and gastrointestinal symptoms were the most frequent autonomic symptoms reported by PD participants in this cohort.
This may reflect SCOPA-AUT structure as there are more GI/urinary questions compared to some other domains, although our focus was on symptom presence.
Most participants experienced persistent urinary symptoms throughout the 60-month observation period, and gastrointestinal dysfunction was similarly prevalent.

These findings align with previous research, including a Chinese cohort study that identified dry mouth (59.26%) and constipation (49.07%) as the most common gastrointestinal symptoms, and urinary urgency and nocturia (35%) as prominent urinary complaints [15].

text.text: The high prevalence of these symptoms in both Western and Chinese populations underscores their central role in the clinical picture of PD.
However, the pattern of autonomic involvement can vary across studies.

text.text: Further research is needed to clarify risk factors, underlying mechanisms, and targeted interventions to alleviate these symptoms and improve patients' quality of life.

While our study confirms a significant progression of both motor and non-motor symptoms over time in PD, as evidenced by the annual changes in MDS-UPDRS II and III scores, we did not find a statistically significant association between the rate of this progression and the number of autonomic symptom complaints at baseline.

This suggests that while autonomic dysfunction and motor symptoms both worsen over time in PD, the severity of autonomic symptoms at baseline does not appear to predict a faster rate of motor decline.
This finding contrasts with some prior studies suggesting a link between autonomic dysfunction and faster disease progression [3].

text.text: However, it is important to note that autonomic dysfunction is highly prevalent in PD [16], and its presence may broadly contribute to disease severity without necessarily influencing the rate of motor decline.

text.text: Further, the absence of statistical significance in the interaction term indicates that the relationship between autonomic dysfunction and motor decline is not uniform and may be influenced by genetic, lifestyle, or comorbid factors, as well as specific patterns of autonomic dysfunction [11].

text.text: Future research is needed to explore the complex interplay between autonomic and motor systems in PD and to identify potential predictors of disease progression.

text.text: Individuals with more than two affected autonomic domains at baseline experienced a steeper decline in cognitive performance, as measured by the MoCA, whereas those with none or one to two affected domains showed no significant change.
Cognitive deterioration in PD is multifactorial, involving dopamine and acetylcholine deficits and the spread of alpha-synuclein pathology to cortical regions [24].

text.text: Since the effect was modest in magnitude in our study, it is best regarded as a group-level signal requiring replication rather than as a clinically actionable prognostic marker.

Despite the PD group having a higher frequency of orthostatic hypotension (OH) and the HC group having a lower frequency, we also found no significant longitudinal differences in the change in presence of OH between PD and HC over 60 months, nor any influence from baseline autonomic symptom severity on the SCOPA-AUT scale, which contrasts with the literature.
Methodological differences may explain this.

For example, Beach and McKay 2024 [26] and Chen et al. 2021 [27] relied on clinical diagnosis in unfiltered PPMI idiopathic PD cohorts without SAA confirmation; our SAA+ restriction ensured more biologically homogeneous early PD with potentially milder profiles.

text.text: These methodological gaps also call for larger, multi-site trials with consistent OH protocols and full biomarker integration to clarify its true role in early disease.

This study's strengths include its longitudinal design and the use of a well-characterized cohort, which enabled the prospective assessment of autonomic dysfunction progression over an extended period.
However, several limitations must be acknowledged.
Reliance on the SCOPA-AUT questionnaire introduces potential recall bias.
The SCOPA-AUT is a screening and severity instrument and is not equivalent to a targeted clinical or laboratory autonomic examination.
Therefore, symptoms that a participant does not perceive will not be reported, producing underascertainment.

Conversely, symptoms may be misinterpreted or misattributed, so that complaints arising from benign prostatic hyperplasia, diabetes, medication effects, or normal aging may be recorded as autonomic in origin, producing over-ascertainment.

Because these sources of misclassification apply to both cohorts, they are likely to be largely non-differential and would tend to attenuate rather than generate the between group differences reported here; nonetheless, all prevalence estimates should be read as approximations.
Antiparkinsonian medications can influence autonomic function [28].
text.formatted: Antiparkinsonian medications can influence autonomic function <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Although statistical models adjusted for medication classes, disentangling drug effects from disease-related autonomic dysfunction remains challenging.
Moreover, adjusting for actual medication dose levels, rather than dichotomized medication classes, would have been an ideal way to account for dynamic changes in medication use over time.
Cardiovascular, metabolic, and urinary comorbiditiesmore common in PD-may confound the observed associations, despite statistical adjustments [11].

text.text: Importantly, substantial attrition occurred over the five-year period.

This raises concern for attrition bias, as those with more severe autonomic symptoms or greater overall disability may have been disproportionately lost to follow-up., As a result, the observed high prevalence of autonomic symptoms should be interpreted cautiously [29].

text.text: Nevertheless, the sensitivity analyses showed that PD participants with and without Year 5 autonomic data did not differ significantly in baseline autonomic symptom severity or in the prevalence in any individual autonomic domain at baseline (Supplementary Table 6), and the IPW-GEE results generally supported the robustness of the primary longitudinal findings (Supplementary Table 7).

text.text: Since heart rate criteria and supine hypertension were not assessed, the OH screening only reflects orthostatic blood pressure, making it impossible to distinguish between neurogenic and nonneurogenic OH.

Lastly, the binary indicator of a total autonomic symptom score >1 is likely influenced by a ceiling effect in the PD cohort (96-98% at every visit) and is also high (87-94% at every visit) among HC participants.

text.text: This limited variability may reduce the ability to detect differences in longitudinal trajectories between the PD and HC groups.
Therefore, these findings should be interpreted with caution as they do not necessarily support specificity of autonomic dysfunction in PD.
